world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Retired ISO bookkeeping entry (merged with Tae' [rob] 2009); no Toala'-specific description surfaced.

new_statements.quote: Moreover, in this case, the stress pattern of Taeq language generally falls on the penultimate syllable of a word, but the stress moves on to a long vowel when it occurs, for instance, the word Jonga (deer), Lalan (road), tEallo (today), lOlang (walk), bUlawang (gold), mawArang (thirsty), karAtasa (research), and kamawAtaKan (power). As seen those words above, the stress is made up from the long vowel and the stress falls penultimate syllable whether the word that has two, three, and four syllables. It also occurs at the level of the word that has affixes. [...] Those examples can be concluded that the rule of stress patterns of Taeq language are determined by the stress falls on penultimate syllable of the word itself.
new_statements.citation: Garing, Jusmianti. 2012. The influence of Taeq language to English on stress patterns produced by Taeq speakers at English Department of Cokroaminoto University Palopo. Sawerigading 18(3): 351-359. Makassar: Balai Bahasa Provinsi Sulawesi Selatan dan Sulawesi Barat.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tae' word stress is regular on the penultimate syllable of the word, in two-, three- and four-syllable words and (per the author) also in affixed words; the stressed vowel is realized long. This agrees with Grimes & Grimes 1987 (PL D-78 p. 94), whose South Sulawesi wordlists, including the Toala'(-Palili') list, leave the default penultimate stress unmarked.
new_statements.exceptions: Author says stress 'moves on to a long vowel when it occurs' without elaborating; several of her own capitalized examples look antepenultimate rather than penultimate (tEallo, bUlawang, karAtasa, kamawAtaKan), and in the next paragraph she marks kamawa'taKan and speaks of a stressed [ta] in the suffixed word, so behaviour with suffixes/paragogic final syllables is not reliably described. Grimes & Grimes 1987's Toala' wordlist marks a handful of non-default stresses with an apostrophe (e.g. ['indete], ['ke?ede], ['me?ese], [ma'tumbai]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolated citation forms; contrastive EFL study by a Balai Bahasa linguist based in Palopo, describing Tae' as a whole (no dialect named), not specifically the Bastem/Toala' variety. No instrumental data; author states no earlier research on Tae' stress exists.
new_statements.identity_note: toal1234 'Toala'' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid for the retired ISO code tlz, merged into Tae' [rob] = taee1237 on 2009-01-16 (ISO 639-3 CR 2008-026). Per that request (following Vail 1991) Toala' = the Bastem subdialect of the South Luwu' dialect of Tae'; Grimes & Grimes 1987's 'Toala'' (dialects Toala' [mountain] and Palili' [coast]) = Valkama 1987's 'Luwu' (WILC 5 p. 127). The quoted stress statement (Garing 2012) describes Tae' as a whole from Palopo, not the Bastem variety specifically, and the same file is the deciding source in the taee1237 folder; to avoid counting one language twice, any catalog entry should be filed under taee1237 (Tae'), with toal1234 cross-referenced to it rather than catalogued as a separate entity.

sources.note: p. 94 (Appendix E conventions): 'Stress in South Sulawesi languages usually occurs on the penultimate syllable. In such cases it is not marked in the word lists. Where stress deviates from the normal pattern.. it is marked with an apostrophe preceding the stressed syllable.' Toala' entry pp. 49-50 (dialects Toala', Palili'); Toala'(-Palili') wordlist TLA taken in Palopo Dec 1982 is mostly unmarked (= penult) with a few apostrophe-marked items (e.g. ['indete], ['ke?ede], ['me?ese], [ma'tumbai]). No Toala'-specific note in the per-language phonetic remarks (pp. 96-97).
